title: AI API Failure Triage
summary: Use HTTP response evidence to classify an AI API failure and choose a safe next action. This intermediate troubleshooting guide distinguishes client, server, gateway, timeout, and rate-limit responses without assuming a specific provider.
prerequisites: The failed request and its HTTP response, if a response was received
Knowledge of whether repeating the request could duplicate an operation

sections.title: Immediate triage
paragraphs: The intermediate practitioner question is: What should I do first when an AI API request fails? Start with the HTTP status and any Retry-After field, classify the response, and retry only when you can determine that repeating the request is safe. If no HTTP response is available, record the outcome as UNKNOWN rather than assigning a status-based cause, preserve the available failure evidence, and investigate whether the request reached an HTTP server before applying this decision path.

Step 1: Record the complete HTTP status and the Retry-After field when the response includes one. If either value cannot be obtained, mark that value UNKNOWN and continue only with evidence that is actually present. Do not infer a missing status from an error message.

Step 2: Classify a 4xx response as a condition in which the client seems to have erred and a 5xx response as a condition in which the server is aware that it has erred or cannot perform the requested method. If the status is outside those classes or its meaning is not established here, mark the classification UNKNOWN and use the response itself as the next diagnostic evidence.

Step 3: Use the specific status when it is available. A 400 response identifies a perceived client error, 401 identifies missing valid authentication credentials, 403 means the server understood the request but refuses to fulfill it, 408 means the server did not receive a complete request in time, and 429 means too many requests were sent in a given period. A 500 response identifies an unexpected server condition, 502 an invalid upstream response received by a gateway or proxy, 503 temporary overload or scheduled maintenance, and 504 an upstream response that did not arrive in time. If the status does not identify the exact defective input or operational cause, treat that detail as UNKNOWN and inspect the response evidence rather than guessing.

Step 4: Choose the next action from the established meaning. Correct the perceived client-side condition before repeating a 400 request. Supply valid authentication credentials before repeating a 401 request. Treat 403 as an understood request that was refused rather than assuming that another authentication attempt will resolve it. For 408, a client may repeat the request on a new connection, but only after applying the retry-safety check. For 429 or 503, follow Retry-After when it is present. For 500, 502, 503, or 504, retain the response as server or intermediary evidence and apply the same retry-safety check before another attempt. If Retry-After is absent, the appropriate delay is UNKNOWN here and must not be invented.

sections.title: Retry safety and source correction
paragraphs: Before an automatic retry, determine whether repeating the request is safe. A method is idempotent when multiple identical requests have the same intended effect as one request. Do not automatically retry a non-idempotent request unless its semantics are known to be idempotent or there is evidence that the original request was not applied. If safety cannot be determined, stop automatic retries and require a review of the original operation before proceeding.

This source correction affects the support available for HTTP status, Retry-After, idempotency, and retry-safety statements. Those statements are supported here by RFC 9110. sections.callout: A retry is a new operation unless you can establish that repeating the request is safe. A transient-looking status alone does not establish retry safety.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: Expected evidence consists of the original HTTP status or an explicit UNKNOWN status, any received Retry-After value, the status-based classification, the selected next action, and a recorded decision about whether repeating the request is safe. Verify the triage by checking that each classification matches the recorded status and that no absent response detail has been inferred.

If a corrective action is applied, compare the follow-up response with the original evidence. For a 400 or 401 response, verify that the identified client-side condition was addressed before another request. For 408, 429, or 503, verify that any retry followed the applicable retry-safety decision and the received Retry-After instruction when one was present. For 500, 502, 503, or 504, verify that the server or intermediary response was retained for further diagnosis.

Triage is complete when the failure has an evidence-backed classification and a safe next action, even if the request has not succeeded. If the follow-up attempt fails with the same status, retain both responses and continue diagnosis without changing the classification unless new evidence supports the change. If it fails with a different status, restart the decision path using the new response.
